title: Developing Evidence-Based Micronutrient Guidelines: An Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine Framework
content: Background: Dietary reference values and many supplementation studies focus on preventing deficiency, maintaining nutritional adequacy, or avoiding excessive exposure. These are essential objectives but do not settle whether altered nutrient requirements, clinically meaningful insufficiency, or distinct pharmacological interventions warrant investigation. Nutrient trials also differ from many drug trials because all participants have pre-existing nutrient exposure and effects can depend on baseline status, achieved concentrations, and biological timing.Objective: To propose a transparent, biologically informed methodology for developing and evaluating micronutrient guidelines across nutritional and therapeutic applications without weakening standards for causal claims, clinical benefit, or safety.Methods: We present a critical narrative synthesis of nutrient-specific trial methodology, dietary reference intakes, toxicology, selected trials, and guideline-development standards. We trace antecedents from Cheng’s 2024 discussion of nutritional versus therapeutic dosing, Grant et al.’s 2025 vitamin D guideline review, and Cheng’s 2026 Nutrient Prioritization preprint; the present framework integrates prior principles and articulates two additional proposed principles [17–19].Framework: The Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine Micronutrient Guideline Development Framework (I-OM-MGDF) integrates the previously described Nutrient Demand and Nutrient Prioritization concepts with two principles newly named and formulated here: Nutrient Safety–Benefit Exploration and the Nutrient Functional–Therapeutic Continuum. Fourteen assessment domains connect physiology, dose, harms, evidence certainty, and recommendation development.Conclusions: Micronutrient guidelines should explicitly separate deficiency prevention, correction of evidence-supported insufficiency, physiological optimization hypotheses, and disease-specific pharmacological treatment. An intake below an identified toxicity threshold is not automatically safe or beneficial, but a biologically plausible, ethically justified exposure can merit rigorous study. Clinical recommendations should target demonstrated net benefit rather than the highest tolerated dose. The I-OM-MGDF is a proposal for subsequent pilot testing, expert appraisal, and validation—not an endorsed or validated practice guideline.
